newsitem.title: POLAND: RUSSIAN DUTIES MAY CURB IMPORTS COMING VIA POLAND.
newsitem.headline: RUSSIAN DUTIES MAY CURB IMPORTS COMING VIA POLAND.

text.p: Russia, while keen to boost trade with Poland, will protect its markets against goods imported via Poland from third countries, Foreign Trade Minister Oleg Davydov said on Friday.
"It will be necessary to examine import customs tariffs so goods from other countries will not reach Russia with Poland acting as intermediary," Davydov told a news conference.

"Russia is ready temporarily to protect its market against goods coming from countries with which Poland has signed free trade agreements," he said in Krynica, southern Poland, during an economic forum involving former Soviet states and Poland.
Davydov also said Russia welcomed Polish investments and would support them in sectors selected by Moscow -- initially this would apply to production of buses and tractors.
Bilateral trade, which slumped after the 1989 fall of communism, has been reviving.
Russia is Poland's third largest trade partner -- 1995 turnover was $3.2 billion, up 35 percent against 1994, with the balance $686 million in Russia's favour.
Exchanges are seen exceeding $4 billion this year, with Poland's exports growing 47 percent and Russia's 20 percent.
Both sides recognise this could expand further but that more trade liberalisation, a proper payments system and an exchange of banking facilities are required.
Bank Handlowy SA, Poland's biggest state-owned commercial bank, and the cooperative giant Bank Gospodarki Zywnosciowej SA (BGZ) are leading the way.

Handlowy, which wants to start banking operations in Russia next year, is seeking a full operational licence, while BGZ aims to create a Polish-Russian bank after setting up a Moscow office with Smolensk and Kaliningrad branches.
Talking of the licences to be issued, Davydov said:
"These banks will be able to carry out not only payments stemming from bilateral trade but also to be active on the stock market and investment funds operating in Russia."
First Deputy Foreign Trade Minister Yurii Grekov said a hurdle was a requirement that foreign capital should not exceed 12 percent -- meaning Polish banks would need Russian partners.
Russia would submit proposals for its banks to operate in Poland by the end of the year, Grekov added.
Davydov said the Central European Free Trade Association (CEFTA) was ill-prepared to develop closer trade with Russia.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin wrote to a summit of the five-member CEFTA in Bratislava last month saying Russia wanted dialogue on possible cooperation and liberalisation of trade with the grouping, although it did not now aspire to join.
But Davydov was lukewarm about prospects for such ties.
"The organisation of CEFTA is structurally too weak for the intensification of foreign exchanges. Mechanisms for cooperation between Russia and CEFTA have not been worked out."

CEFTA, linking the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia, agreed last month on liberalisation of trade covering industrial products, standards for rules on origin of goods and expansion of the group, which plans to admit Romania next year.
